lesson.title: Teaching Your Objects to Introduce Themselves
lesson.summary: __str__ controls what print() and str() show for your object: a readable, human-facing description instead of a cryptic default.
lesson.body:
Try building an object from a class that defines no special display behavior, and printing it.

```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

point = Point(3, 4)
print(point)
```

This prints something like <__main__.Point object at 0x104b1f110>. That hexadecimal number is a memory address, and it is technically true (it does identify the object) but useless to a person reading your program's output. It tells you nothing about what the point actually is.

The __str__ dunder method fixes this. When you call print(obj) or str(obj), Python looks for a __str__ method on obj's class and, if it finds one, uses whatever string that method returns instead of the default.

```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"

point = Point(3, 4)
print(point)
print(str(point))
```

Both lines print (3, 4). The f-string inside __str__ builds a readable description using the object's own attributes, and print() and str() both route through that same method.

Think of __str__ as the answer to "how should this look to a person using the program," the way you would describe the object out loud. If you were building a Card class for a game, __str__ might return "Queen of Hearts" rather than something that reveals internal implementation details, like which numeric rank or suit code you happen to be storing. The goal is readability, not completeness or precision.

One rule worth remembering now, even though the next chapter covers it in depth: __str__ is not the only display method Python supports. There is a second one, __repr__, meant for a different audience, other programmers debugging your code, rather than end users reading program output. If a class defines __repr__ but not __str__, print() and str() will fall back to using __repr__, since Python treats __repr__ as the more fundamental of the two. But if you want a friendly, plain-language description specifically for display, __str__ is the method to write.
